title: Introduction to Analog Design
intro: Almost every system that touches the real world needs analog circuits at its edge: they sense, amplify, filter and convert signals that no digital gate can handle directly.

blocks.text: The world is analog: light, sound, temperature, radio waves and chemical concentrations are continuous quantities. A sensor turns one into a small voltage or current, and that signal has to be amplified, filtered and digitised before any digital logic can use it. The more of the system lives in digital, the more it depends on a thin, careful layer of analog at the boundaries.

items: Sensing and processing: microphones, image sensors, accelerometers and radio antennas deliver microvolt to millivolt signals buried in noise.

Digital signals become analog: a fast bit stream on a long wire or backplane is really an analog waveform with finite rise time, ringing and noise. High-speed links therefore need equalisers, clock recovery and careful receivers.
Analog design is in demand: it is hard to automate, does not scale as easily as logic, and every new interface standard needs new analog front ends.
The challenge: analog circuits trade off many quantities at once, and no single metric can be optimised alone.

blocks.text: Almost every analog block is judged on the same set of competing specifications: gain, bandwidth, power dissipation, supply voltage, linearity, noise, maximum voltage swing and input/output impedance. Improving one usually costs another. This 'analog design octagon' is the mental model that the rest of this topic keeps returning to.

Putting analog circuits on the same chip as digital ones lowers cost, shrinks size and power, and removes the capacitance and inductance of package pins and board traces that would otherwise limit speed. The price is that integrated components are imperfect: resistors and capacitors vary by 10 to 30 percent, there are no good inductors in plain CMOS, and the substrate couples noise between blocks.

CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) technology dominates because digital logic, memory and analog can share one process, and because scaling transistors down has made them cheaper and faster every generation. Bipolar and BiCMOS processes still offer higher gm per unit current and better matching, but the economics favour CMOS.
Analog design moves between several levels, and a good designer can jump between them:

items: System: what the product has to do (a receiver, a data converter).
Architecture: how the blocks connect (amplifier, filter, converter, PLL).
Circuit: the transistor-level schematic of each block.
Device: the physics of one transistor, including parasitics.
Layout and process: the geometry and fabrication that realise the circuit.

blocks.text: This topic climbs that ladder: device physics first, then single-stage amplifiers, then multi-stage circuits and feedback, and finally larger blocks (references, oscillators, PLLs) and the realities of layout.

How to study this topic: read the page, play with the simulation, then try each problem before you open its hidden solution. Equations are written in plain text: gm is transconductance, ro output resistance, Vov overdrive voltage, || means parallel resistance.

blocks.title: Which spec would you trade?
blocks.text: A battery-powered ECG amplifier has to detect 1 mV signals. Name two octagon specifications you would deliberately relax to gain the others, and justify.
solution: Biomedical front ends care most about noise and power. Bandwidth is only about 100 Hz, so you can use very low bias currents (low power) and small bandwidth to integrate less noise. Speed and output swing can be relaxed: the signal is slow, and later stages handle larger swing.
In general you relax whichever specifications the application does not need, then spend the saved power or area on the ones that matter.
blocks.answer: Relax speed (bandwidth) and swing; spend on noise and power.
